title: "Open modes"
description: "Classic rasters (bands as a dimension or as variables) and multidimensional arrays."
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
from _common import *
import json
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

`gdalxarray` opens a source in one of two GDAL data models, chosen by
`multidim=`:

| | `multidim=False` (classic) | `multidim=True` (default) |
|---|---|---|
| GDAL API | `gdal.Open`, raster bands | `gdal.OpenEx(..., OF_MULTIDIM_RASTER)`, groups and arrays |
| Dimensions | `(band, y, x)` | whatever the source names: `time`, `depth`, `lat`, `lon`, ... |
| Georeferencing | geotransform + CRS, as a `RasterIndex` and `CRSIndex` | coordinate arrays from the source |
| Natural for | GeoTIFF/COG, JPEG2000, classic VRT, warped VRT | netCDF, HDF5, Zarr, GRIB, multidim VRT, Icechunk |

## Classic, bands as a dimension

The default for `multidim=False`: one `band_data` variable with
dimensions `(band, y, x)`, the layout rioxarray uses. The example is a
cloud-free Sentinel-2 summer scene over Hobart, from kunanyi / Mount
Wellington to the Derwent estuary: four bands (blue, green, red, near
infrared) on the scene's own UTM zone 55S grid, averaged to 20 m.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
provenance("sentinel2")
```

```{python}
src = data("sentinel2/" + data_json("sentinel2/provenance.json")["file"])
ds = xr.open_dataset(src, engine="gdalxarray", multidim=False)
ds
```

The cell coordinates come from the geotransform, and the CRS rides on
the `crs` coordinate's index:

```{python}
ds.xindexes["crs"]
```

The bands are stored as integers with a scale and offset (Sentinel-2
L2A digital numbers); with the default `mask_and_scale=True` they arrive
as surface reflectance, with nodata masked:

```{python}
ds["band_data"].encoding.get("scale_factor"), ds["band_data"].encoding.get("add_offset"), \
    float(ds["band_data"].mean())
```

Ordinary xarray operations apply. A true-colour composite is a
selection and reordering along `band`:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Sentinel-2 true colour (red, green, blue reflectance, stretched) over Hobart, kunanyi / Mount Wellington and the Derwent estuary."
rgb = ds["band_data"].sel(band=[3, 2, 1])               # red, green, blue
rgb = (rgb / rgb.quantile(0.98)).clip(0, 1).transpose("y", "x", "band")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6.7))
rgb.plot.imshow(ax=ax, rgb="band")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_title("true colour, " + data_json("sentinel2/provenance.json")["day"])
ax.set_xlabel("easting (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("northing (m)")
plt.show()
```

## Classic, bands as variables

`band_as_dim=False` makes each band its own variable, named from the
band description (or `band_N` when there is none). This suits rasters
whose bands are different quantities, and makes band arithmetic read
like the quantities it combines:

```{python}
dsv = xr.open_dataset(src, engine="gdalxarray", multidim=False, band_as_dim=False)
list(dsv.data_vars), dsv["nir"].dims
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Normalised difference vegetation index, (nir - red) / (nir + red), computed from the named band variables."
ndvi = (dsv["nir"] - dsv["red"]) / (dsv["nir"] + dsv["red"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6.7))
ndvi.plot(ax=ax, cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=-0.5, vmax=0.9, cbar_kwargs={"label": "NDVI"})
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_title("NDVI")
ax.set_xlabel("easting (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("northing (m)")
plt.show()
```

## Multidimensional

For sources with their own dimensions. The fixture below is a
ROMS-style ocean model history file written as Zarr v3: a vertical
`s_rho` axis, two index dimensions, 2D longitude and latitude arrays,
and the scalar parameters of the vertical transform.

```{python}
roms = xr.open_dataset(fixture("index/roms-fan.zarr"), engine="gdalxarray")
roms
```

Dimensions, coordinates and attributes come from the store, so
selection reads like the model's own description:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Temperature on the surface level and the deepest level of the fan grid, by index."
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 4.5), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, k, name in [(axs[0], -1, "surface"), (axs[1], 0, "bottom")]:
    roms["temp"].isel(s_rho=k).plot(ax=ax, cmap="RdYlBu_r", vmin=float(roms.temp.min()),
                                     vmax=float(roms.temp.max()), add_colorbar=(k == 0))
    ax.set_title(f"{name} (s_rho = {float(roms.s_rho[k]):.2f})")
plt.show()
```

Placing these cells on the earth uses the 2D `lon_rho` and `lat_rho`
arrays; see [Curvilinear grids](curvilinear.qmd).

## Checked against GDAL

The three Zarr fixtures in wxylib/fixtures hold the same pixels as
three of the COGs, and their manifest lists windows whose values GDAL
read with `osgeo.gdal`. gdalxarray must give the same numbers through
xarray indexing, in both modes:

```{python}
man = fixture_json("zarr/manifest.json")
rows = []
for case in man["cases"]:
    path = fixture("zarr/" + case["store"])
    md = xr.open_dataset(path, engine="gdalxarray", mask_and_scale=False)[case["array"]]
    cl = xr.open_dataset(f'ZARR:"{path}":/{case["array"]}', engine="gdalxarray",
                         multidim=False, mask_and_scale=False)["band_data"]
    for w in case["windows"]:
        win = dict(y=slice(w["row"], w["row"] + w["height"]),
                   x=slice(w["col"], w["col"] + w["width"]))
        expect = fixture_array("zarr/" + w["file"], case["dtype"])
        a = md.isel(**win).values
        b = cl.isel(**win).values
        ok_md = np.array_equal(a.ravel(), expect)
        ok_cl = np.array_equal(b.ravel(), expect)
        rows.append((case["store"], w["file"].rsplit("/", 1)[-1], a.shape, ok_md, ok_cl))
        assert ok_md and ok_cl, (case["store"], w["file"])

import pandas as pd
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["store", "oracle window", "shape", "multidim", "classic"])
```
